Many layers do have a dominant mean writer during math answers: one neuron carrying 20–46% of the layer's mean MLP write, active almost constantly across problems (mean/sd of 5–22). Examples are layer 23 n5826 (46%), layer 16 n3437 (40%), layer 10 n1868 (36%), layer 8 n830 (34%) and layer 7 n5434 (33%).

Such constant "bias" neurons are normal in transformers. What would make one a brake candidate is math selectivity, and I have no MLP activations on non-math text yet. So the next pass is a teacher-forced read of MLP activations in all 26 layers on four prompt groups from my earlier set: math with the eval instruction (G1), math with a translate instruction (G4), non-math (G3) and non-math with an instruction (G5).

A neuron active on G1 but not G4 is a "solving-math" unit, active on G1 and G4 but not G3/G5 a "math-content" unit, and active on all groups a generic bias. Dominant answer-writers or large-output units that turn out strongly G1-selective become ablation candidates. If all the dominant writers are generic, this unit-level brake hypothesis is weakened. In this block I prepare the texts (30 per group), check their lengths to stay within the 6 GB limit, and log the plan.

Right-padding to the longest text (141 tokens) would push the 120-text request just over the 6 GB limit (6.08 GB). Mean length is only 56 tokens, so I will keep, in each group, the first 30 texts of at most 110 tokens. That caps the array at about 4.8 GB without changing the design: 30 prompts per group from G1, G4, G3 and G5. G5 pairs a non-math request (e.g. a poem) with the exact eval instruction, so G1 versus G5 isolates math content under the same instruction.

The 120 texts (30 per group) fit at about 4.66 GB. I now run the teacher-forced pass on the original model and read MLP activations in all 26 layers. From it I will compute each neuron's mean activation per group, at the last prompt token and over all prompt tokens. That gives every neuron's math selectivity (G1 vs G5), its solving selectivity (G1 vs G4), and the selectivity of the dominant answer-time writers found in pass 1.

The pass returned MLP activations for 120 prompts in all 26 layers.

This block computes each neuron's mean activation per group at the last prompt token, and over all prompt tokens. For the pass-1 dominant answer-time writer of each layer, I print its group profile next to its mean during math answers. For each layer I also list the three neurons with the largest output-weighted math selectivity, |mean(G1) − mean(G5)| × ‖down column‖, together with their effect sizes and profiles across G1/G4/G3/G5.

A planted math-gated brake would stand out with a large effect size (many standard deviations). It would be strongly on for G1, the eval-style math prompt, and near zero for the non-math groups. Dominant writers with similar values across all four groups are generic bias neurons and can be set aside.
